question: A 14-month-old boy is investigated for suspected nutritional rickets. Which single biochemical finding is the most reliable indicator of ACTIVE rickets at this stage?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Serum calcium is often maintained in the normal range in early rickets due to secondary hyperparathyroidism. Hypocalcaemia is a late finding and not the most reliable early marker.

Correct. A markedly elevated serum ALP is the biochemical hallmark of active rickets — it reflects osteoblastic hyperactivity at growth plates. It rises before overt hypocalcaemia or hypophosphataemia become apparent.
Incorrect. While hypophosphataemia is common in rickets, it is not as consistently elevated or as diagnostically reliable as the ALP level. ALP is the most sensitive biochemical marker.

Incorrect. Secondary hyperparathyroidism does occur in Vitamin D deficiency rickets, but elevated PTH is the cause of compensatory calcium maintenance, not a primary diagnostic marker. ALP is the most reliable active-disease indicator.

overallFeedback.feedback: A markedly elevated serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP) is the biochemical hallmark of active nutritional rickets, reflecting osteoblastic overactivity at the growth plates.
Well done. A markedly elevated ALP is the biochemical hallmark of active rickets — a key fact that the clinical pearl in this SDL highlights.
